newsitem.title: UK: Urals shrug off Iraq price cut, but may soon slide.
newsitem.headline: Urals shrug off Iraq price cut, but may soon slide.

text.p: A cut in the European price of Iraqi crude is unlikely to dent the value of its Russian rival in the short term, but it may pressure Moscow's Urals grade as April approaches, oil traders said on Monday.
"I would see Urals at Dated (Brent) -$1.10/-$1.15 in the very short term," said a trader.
"But definitely there will be pressure in the medium term. I see it coming off to (Dated minus) $1.30 or $1.35 -- barring other news or manipulation of the market."
At the weekend Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) confirmed to European buyers a 25-cent reduction in the formula for its Kirkuk crude, loaded at Turkey's Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.
Kirkuk will be priced at Dated Brent less $1.80 fob Ceyhan from March 10 when the second 90-day period of the United Nations six-month oil-for-food exchange began.
Kirkuk for April would be priced at Dated Brent less $1.90 fob, reflecting a 10-cent reduction in the price of competitor crude Saudi Arab Light for the month.

Traders said Urals would enjoy a degree of insulation from the Kirkuk adjustment this week because the Russian grade was almost sold out for March and Urals' April loading programme had not yet been published.

"It's still at (Brent) -$1.15," one trader insisted. "There are almost no cargoes available for March and probably one short. Plus there are a couple of people who can't take Urals because of the sulphur content. So it looks stable."

But other traders said Urals and other grades traded on the spot market could eventually feel pressure from April Kirkuk barrels and buyers attracted by the lower formula show greater readiness to lift Kirkuk.

They said that with Urals currently priced about Dated Brent less $1.15 it has been difficult to find buyers for Kirkuk. The bigger discount was the only way to ensure traders lift all their contracted volumes.
Some buyers, resisting the old Kirkuk formula, had sought to postpone lifting dates to May.
"A 25-cent cut will not alter the economics at the refinery greatly but there will be less resistance from buyers wanting to lift Kirkuk," a trader said.
Iraqi crude formulas are priced against regional benchmark crudes for Asia, Europe and the U.S. and moved in line with changes to Arab Light to each region.

But a key unknown remains the effect of the lower price on Iraqi sales volumes. Lower prices mean Baghdad has to sell more oil to meet its $1 billion target for the second 90 days of the oil-for-food deal.

And as long as Iraq continues to operate under a revenue ceiling in a weak market, sales increases are likely to chase falling prices in a vicious circle that could help bring the whole oil complex lower, traders said.
At current prices Iraq would have to export about 650,000 bpd to raise a $1 billion by June 9 in the second 90 days of the U.N. deal.
"In fact the Iraqi cut might be too little too late. While the pressure will be on Urals, fundamentally it's the same weak market all over the Med," the trader said.
He noted a trade on Friday of Syrian Light at Dated -92 cents, 42 cents under the official selling price.

Another potential casualty of the Iraqi alteration could be Saudi Light. While it is sold on term contracts, its May formula may have to be adjusted lower to fend off competition from a lower-priced Kirkuk, traders said.
